title: Mensuration (2D)
summary: Areas and perimeters of triangles, quadrilaterals, circles, sectors and regular polygons, plus paths, wheels and percentage-change effects. A reliable 1-3 questions per shift; the formulas are few and heavily recycled, so this converts to marks faster than almost any other advanced topic.

subtopics.title: Areas of triangles
subtopics.concept: Area of a triangle is half of base times height, and any side can be the base. Equilateral, isosceles and right triangles have shortcuts that turn most exam questions into one line. Heron's formula covers everything else using only the three sides.

mistakes.wrong: Using the slant side as the height.
mistakes.right: The height is perpendicular to the base. In the 17-17-16 triangle it is 15, not 17.

mistakes.wrong: Forgetting to halve the base in an isosceles triangle.
mistakes.right: Pythagoras needs the half-base 8, so the height is $\sqrt{289-64}=15$.

mistakes.wrong: Running Heron on a right triangle.
mistakes.right: A triplet like 6-8-10 needs only $\dfrac{6\times8}{2}=24$.

mistakes.wrong: Using the full perimeter as $s$.
mistakes.right: $s$ is the half-perimeter. For 13-14-15, $s=21$, not 42.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing the legs with the hypotenuse in $h=\dfrac{ab}{c}$.
mistakes.right: $c$ is the hypotenuse. Legs 6 and 8 over 10 give $h=4.8$.

subtopics.notes:
### One master formula
$$K=\frac{1}{2}\times\text{base}\times\text{height}$$
The height is the perpendicular dropped onto the chosen base. Pick the side whose height is easiest, then stick with that pair.

Two triangles on the same base and between the same parallels always have equal areas. Half of the same base and the same height forces the same area. A median uses exactly that, which is why it never fails to halve a triangle.

> **Rule:** Any side may be the base, but the height must be measured perpendicular to that exact side.

### The three special triangles
- **Right triangle**: the two legs act as base and height. Legs $6$ and $8$ give $K=\dfrac{6\times8}{2}=24$, hypotenuse $10$.
- **Equilateral** (side $a$): height $=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}a$, area $=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{4}a^2$. Side $12$: height $6\sqrt3$, area $36\sqrt3$.
- **Isosceles**: the median to the base is the height. Equal sides $17$, base $16$: half-base $8$, height $\sqrt{289-64}=15$, area $\dfrac{16\times15}{2}=120$.

> **Tip:** Equilateral numbers stay clean: for $a=6$ the area is $9\sqrt3$, and every side gives a multiple of $\sqrt3$.

### Heron's formula
With all three sides, take the half-perimeter first:
$$s=\frac{a+b+c}{2},\qquad K=\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$$
Sides $13$, $14$, $15$: $s=21$, so $K=\sqrt{21\times8\times7\times6}=\sqrt{7056}=84$.

Sides $5$, $12$, $13$ give $s=15$ and $K=\sqrt{15\times10\times3\times2}=30$. But $5$-$12$-$13$ is a triplet, so $\dfrac{5\times12}{2}=30$ was faster.

> **Shortcut:** Spot a Pythagorean triplet and skip Heron. A right triangle's area is just half the product of its legs.

### Altitude to the hypotenuse: two areas
The right triangle with legs $6$, $8$ has hypotenuse $10$ and area $24$. Take the hypotenuse as the base instead:
$$\frac{1}{2}\times10\times h=24 \Rightarrow h=4.8=\frac{24}{5}$$
Same triangle, same area, second route. That is the whole trick.

> **Watch:** Equate the two area expressions before touching square roots. The altitude rule $h=\dfrac{ab}{c}$ falls out of it.

### Radii and the median split
- Inradius $r=\dfrac{K}{s}$. For $13$-$14$-$15$: $r=\dfrac{84}{21}=4$.
- Circumradius $R=\dfrac{abc}{4K}=\dfrac{2730}{336}=\dfrac{65}{8}=8.125$.
- Every median splits a triangle into two equal areas. Two medians cut it into four equal areas.
- Equilateral: $R=2r$, and $a=6$ gives $r=\sqrt3$, $R=2\sqrt3$.

> **Remember:** Small radius $r$ divides the area by the half-perimeter; big radius $R$ multiplies the sides. $R=2r$ only in the equilateral case.

subtopics.title: Areas of quadrilaterals
subtopics.concept: A rectangle, square, parallelogram, rhombus or trapezium each has a two-part area formula. Most questions give two facts and ask for a third, so the fast route is an identity, not a quadratic. Any quadrilateral splits into two triangles along a diagonal.

tricks.body: No special shape? Draw one diagonal. The area is half the diagonal times the sum of the two heights.

mistakes.wrong: Treating the slant side of a parallelogram as the height.
mistakes.right: Height is perpendicular. Sides 10 and 8 at $30^\circ$ give area $10\times8\times\dfrac12=40$.

mistakes.wrong: Using $d_1d_2$ for the rhombus area.
mistakes.right: The formula has the half: $\dfrac{1}{2}\times10\times24=120$, not 240.

mistakes.wrong: Halving only one diagonal of a rhombus.
mistakes.right: Both diagonals bisect each other, so both become halves: 5 and 12.

mistakes.wrong: Solving a quadratic for $l$ and $b$ when only $lb$ is asked.
mistakes.right: Use $(l+b)^2-(l^2+b^2)=2lb$ and stop at the product.

mistakes.wrong: Adding the parallel sides after multiplying by the height.
mistakes.right: Trapezium area is $\dfrac12(a+b)h$; add first, then halve and multiply.

subtopics.notes:
### The family card
| Figure | Area | Extras |
|---|---|---|
| Rectangle $l\times b$ | $lb$ | $P=2(l+b)$, diagonal $\sqrt{l^2+b^2}$ |
| Square, side $a$ | $a^2$ | diagonal $a\sqrt2$ |
| Parallelogram | $bh$ or $ab\sin\theta$ | adjacent angles add to $180^\circ$ |
| Rhombus | $\dfrac{1}{2}d_1d_2$ | diagonals cross at $90^\circ$ |
| Trapezium | $\dfrac{1}{2}(a+b)h$ | $a$, $b$ parallel |

> **Rule:** Any quadrilateral: $K=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\text{diagonal}\times(\text{sum of the two perpendiculars on it})$. Every row above is a special case.

### Rectangle from two facts
Given $P=34$ and diagonal $13$: $l+b=17$ and $l^2+b^2=169$. Use the identity
$$(l+b)^2=l^2+b^2+2lb \Rightarrow 289=169+2lb \Rightarrow lb=60$$
Area $60$ without ever finding $l$ and $b$. Check: $l+b=17$ with $lb=60$ gives sides $12$ and $5$, and $5$-$12$-$13$ confirms the diagonal.

A square of side $a$ has diagonal $a\sqrt2$. Given the diagonal $8\sqrt2$, the side is $8$ and the area is $64$.

> **Tip:** Two facts about a rectangle almost always combine through $(l+b)^2$ or $(l-b)^2$. Avoid solving a quadratic.

### Rhombus through half-diagonals
The diagonals bisect each other at right angles, so the halves and one side form a right triangle.

Diagonals in ratio $5:12$ with area $120$: $\dfrac{1}{2}(5k)(12k)=120$ gives $k=2$, so diagonals $10$ and $24$. Halves $5$ and $12$ give side $13$ and perimeter $52$. All four sides are equal, so the perimeter is always four times one side.

> **Watch:** Halves of rhombus diagonals are triplets in disguise: (5, 12, 13), (8, 6, 10), (12, 35, 37).

### Parallelogram and trapezium
Parallelogram sides $10$ and $8$ with a $30^\circ$ angle between them: $K=10\times8\times\sin30^\circ=80\times\dfrac{1}{2}=40$.

Trapezium: parallel sides differ by $8$, height $6$, area $96$. Then $\dfrac{1}{2}(a+b)\times6=96$ gives $a+b=32$; with $a-b=8$, the sides are $20$ and $12$. The height on the base $10$ above is $8\sin30^\circ=4$ cm, and the midsegment between the slanted sides is $\dfrac{20+12}{2}=16$.

> **Remember:** The height of a parallelogram is perpendicular to the base, never the slant side.

### Split along a diagonal
A general quadrilateral with diagonal $12$ and perpendiculars $5$ and $9$ dropping onto it from the other two corners:
$$K=\frac{1}{2}\times12\times(5+9)=84$$
The diagonal makes two triangles; add their two areas to finish.

> **Tip:** A square with diagonal $8\sqrt2$ has side $8$, area $64$. Match the diagonal formula $a\sqrt2$ backwards to the side.

revision: Rectangle: $lb$, $2(l+b)$, $\sqrt{l^2+b^2}$; two facts combine through an identity.
Square: diagonal $a\sqrt2$; backwards from the diagonal, divide by $\sqrt2$.

subtopics.title: Circles, sectors and rings
subtopics.concept: A circle of radius r has area pi times r squared and circumference two pi r, with pi as 22/7 on these exams. Sectors, arcs, rings and wheels are fractions of those two formulas. Quadrants and semicircles are just sectors of 90 and 180 degrees.

mistakes.wrong: Using the diameter as $r$.
mistakes.right: Diameter 70 means $r=35$. Halve before squaring.

mistakes.wrong: Taking $\pi$ as 3.14 when the numbers are multiples of 7.
mistakes.right: Radius 7, 14, 21, 35 with $\pi=\dfrac{22}{7}$ cancels the 7s cleanly.

subtopics.notes:
### The two core formulas
$$K=\pi r^2,\qquad C=2\pi r$$
Use $\pi=\dfrac{22}{7}$ unless the paper says otherwise. Radius first, everything after is arithmetic. Halve any diameter before squaring; the formulas live on the radius.

Circumference $132$ cm: $r=\dfrac{132\times7}{2\times22}=21$, so $K=\dfrac{22}{7}\times441=1386$ sq cm.

> **Rule:** Every circle question starts by fixing $r$. Reverse questions divide by $2\pi$ to get it.

### Sectors and arcs
A sector is a pizza slice; the arc is its crust. Both take the fraction $\dfrac{\theta}{360}$ of the full shape:
$$\text{arc}=\frac{\theta}{360}\times2\pi r,\qquad \text{sector area}=\frac{\theta}{360}\times\pi r^2$$
Radius $35$, angle $72^\circ$: arc $=\dfrac{72}{360}\times220=44$ cm, sector $=\dfrac{72}{360}\times3850=770$ sq cm.

Perimeter of a sector adds the two radii: $44+70=114$ cm. A $90^\circ$ sector of the same circle has arc $\dfrac14\times220=55$ cm and perimeter $55+70=125$ cm.

A ring between radii $17.5$ and $10.5$: $R^2-r^2=306.25-110.25=196$, so $K=\dfrac{22}{7}\times196=616$ sq cm. Difference of squares keeps it clean.

> **Tip:** $\dfrac{72}{360}=\dfrac15$. Simplify the fraction before multiplying; big numbers shrink fast.

### Rings and rolling wheels
A ring between radii $R$ and $r$ has area $\pi(R^2-r^2)$. Outer $14$, inner $7$: $\dfrac{22}{7}\times147=462$ sq cm.

A wheel of diameter $70$ cm covers $C=\dfrac{22}{7}\times70=220$ cm per turn. Rolling $231$ m $=23100$ cm:
$$\text{revolutions}=\frac{23100}{220}=105$$
The reverse works too: $150$ turns cover $150\times220=33000$ cm, which is $330$ m.

> **Watch:** Convert metres to centimetres before dividing. The wheel diameter is in centimetres.

### Circles and squares together
- Circle **inscribed** in a square: diameter $=$ square side. Side $14$ gives $r=7$ and $K=154$.
- Square **inside** a circle: the square's diagonal is the circle's diameter.

> **Remember:** Inscribed means the circle touches all four sides from inside, so side and diameter match.

### Quadrants and semicircles
A quadrant is a quarter circle ($90^\circ$), a semicircle half ($180^\circ$). Same fraction rules.

Quadrant with $r=14$: area $=\dfrac{1}{4}\times\dfrac{22}{7}\times196=154$ sq cm. Arc $=\dfrac14\times88=22$ cm, so its perimeter is $14+14+22=50$ cm. A semicircle with $r=7$ has area $\dfrac12\times154=77$ sq cm and perimeter $14+22=36$ cm.

> **Tip:** Perimeter of a quadrant is two radii plus the quarter arc. Semicircle: two radii make a diameter, plus the half arc.

subtopics.title: Regular polygons and inscribed figures
subtopics.concept: A regular polygon has equal sides and equal angles, so one side length fixes everything. The regular hexagon is the star: it is six equilateral triangles glued together. Exterior angles, interior angles and diagonal counts all come from the number of sides alone.

mistakes.wrong: Using $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{4}a^2$ once for the hexagon.
mistakes.right: That is one triangle. Six of them give $\dfrac{3\sqrt3}{2}a^2$.

mistakes.wrong: Interior angle $=\dfrac{360}{n}$.
mistakes.right: That is the exterior. Interior $=180-\dfrac{360}{n}$; for an octagon, $135^\circ$.

mistakes.wrong: Forgetting to halve $n(n-3)$.
mistakes.right: Each diagonal was counted from both ends: $d=\dfrac{n(n-3)}{2}$.

mistakes.wrong: Longest hexagon diagonal taken as $a\sqrt3$.
mistakes.right: $a\sqrt3$ is the short one; the longest through the centre is $2a$.

mistakes.wrong: Using the side as the apothem.
mistakes.right: The apothem is centre to the middle of a side; hexagon apothem $=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}a$.

subtopics.notes:
### Hexagon: six equilateral triangles
Join the centre to all six corners. Six equilateral triangles of side $a$ appear, so
$$K=\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}a^2 = 6\times\frac{\sqrt3}{4}a^2$$
Side $6$ cm: each small triangle has area $9\sqrt3$, total $54\sqrt3$ sq cm.

Given a hexagon perimeter instead, divide by $6$ first: perimeter $36$ cm means side $6$ cm and area $54\sqrt3$ sq cm.

A regular octagon has area $2(1+\sqrt2)a^2$. Side $4$ cm gives $32+32\sqrt2$ sq cm, but the six-triangle picture is the one that pays off weekly.

> **Rule:** Hexagon side, radius (centre to corner) and side are equal: $R=a$. The apothem is $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}a$.

### Any regular polygon from perimeter and apothem
$$K=\frac{1}{2}\times\text{perimeter}\times\text{apothem}$$
The apothem is the perpendicular from the centre to a side. Perimeter $72$ cm, apothem $6$ cm: $K=\dfrac{1}{2}\times72\times6=216$ sq cm.

For the hexagon of side $6$: apothem $=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\times6=3\sqrt3$, and $\dfrac12\times36\times3\sqrt3=54\sqrt3$, matching the six triangles. Two routes, one answer.

### Slices from the centre
Join the centre of any regular polygon to its corners. You get $n$ identical slices, each an isosceles triangle with apex angle $\dfrac{360^\circ}{n}$. That single picture generates the exterior angle, the apothem (slice height) and the area formula at once.

> **Tip:** This one formula fits every regular polygon, hexagon included. It is the triangle formula applied to all the slices.

### Angles from the side count
- Each exterior angle $=\dfrac{360^\circ}{n}$ (the turn at each corner while walking the boundary).
- Each interior angle $=180^\circ-$ exterior.
- Interior angle sum $=(n-2)\times180^\circ$.

Octagon: exterior $=\dfrac{360}{8}=45^\circ$, interior $=135^\circ$, angle sum $=6\times180^\circ=1080^\circ$.

Pentagon: exterior $72^\circ$, interior $108^\circ$, sum $540^\circ$. Decagon: exterior $36^\circ$, interior $144^\circ$. Reverse works too: interior $144^\circ$ means exterior $36^\circ$, so $n=\dfrac{360}{36}=10$.

> **Watch:** The regular polygon interior angles are equal, so divide the sum by $n$ to check one angle.

### Counting diagonals
From each corner, $n-3$ diagonals leave (skip itself and two neighbours). Each diagonal has two ends:
$$d=\frac{n(n-3)}{2}$$
A polygon with $90$ diagonals: $n^2-3n-180=0$, which factors as $(n-15)(n+12)=0$, so $n=15$.

Small counts are worth memorising: hexagon $9$, pentagon $5$, octagon $20$, decagon $35$.

### Hexagon special lengths
- Longest diagonal (through the centre) $=2a$. Side $8$ gives $16$.
- Short diagonal (skipping one corner) $=a\sqrt3$.

> **Remember:** In a hexagon, side $=$ radius and the longest diagonal $=$ diameter $=2a$. Both fall out of the six triangles picture.

subtopics.title: Percentage change, similarity and re-bent shapes
subtopics.concept: When a shape grows by a scale factor k, every length multiplies by k but every area multiplies by k squared. For percentage changes the master formula is a + b + ab/100. The same wire bent into different shapes encloses different areas, and the circle always wins.

formulas.note: Lengths take k once; areas take k squared.

mistakes.right: Side ratio $3:5$ gives area ratio $9:25$. Square the length ratio.

subtopics.notes:
### Lengths scale once, areas twice
Similar figures with a length ratio $k$ have an area ratio $k^2$. Perimeters are lengths, so they take $k$ too.

Perimeters $3:5$ mean areas $9:25$. If the larger area is $200$ sq cm, the smaller is $200\times\dfrac{9}{25}=72$ sq cm. Multiply by the ratio; never subtract a guessed difference.

Going from areas back to lengths means a square root: areas $9:25$ give sides $3:5$. Two circles with areas $154$ and $616$ sq cm are in ratio $1:4$, so their radii are in ratio $1:2$.

> **Rule:** Square going from lengths to areas; take the root going back. This single line is half the subtopic.

### The percentage change master formula
For two successive percentage changes $a$ and $b$:
$$\text{net}=a+b+\frac{ab}{100}$$
Side $+20\%$: area $=20+20+\dfrac{400}{100}=+44\%$. Side $-10\%$: area $=-10-10+\dfrac{100}{100}=-19\%$.

Reverse it by factoring: area $+21\%$ means the side grew by $10\%$, because $1.21=1.1^2$.

> **Watch:** A $20\%$ side increase is a $44\%$ area increase, not $40\%$. The cross term is what the options try to hide.

### Costs and tiles scale with area
A square room of side $5$ m costs Rs $600$ to carpet. A similar room of side $15$ m has $k=3$, so area is $9$ times and cost is $600\times9=$ Rs $5400$.

Tiles ask the same: divide the floor area by one tile's area, then multiply by the rate. A floor of $6$ m by $4$ m carries $24$ sq m $=240{,}000$ sq cm; tiles of $20\times20$ cm cover $400$ sq cm each, so $600$ tiles.

Numbers to trust: side ratio $2:3$ gives cost ratio $4:9$. A Rs $500$ job grows to Rs $1125$ at that scale, since $500\times\dfrac{9}{4}=1125$.

> **Tip:** Never scale money by the side ratio. Money follows area, so it takes $k^2$.

### Maps, models and enlargements
A map scale $1:5000$ makes lengths $5000$ times bigger, so areas grow by $5000^2=25{,}000{,}000$. A $4$ sq cm plot is $10^8$ sq cm in truth, which is $10{,}000$ sq m ($1$ sq m $=10^4$ sq cm).

> **Remember:** Square the map scale for areas, then convert units once at the end.

### Same wire, different shapes
A $44$ cm wire bent into a circle gives $r=\dfrac{44}{2\pi}=7$ cm, area $154$ sq cm. Bent into a square, side $11$ cm, area $121$ sq cm.

For a fixed perimeter, the circle encloses the most area; among rectangles, the square wins. Equilateral beats every other triangle. Order the options by shape generosity when the question says 'maximum area'.

> **Watch:** Compare areas only after converting the perimeter into each shape's own dimensions.

revision: Length ratio $k$ gives area ratio $k^2$; perimeters take $k$ once.
Two successive changes: $a+b+\dfrac{ab}{100}$; $+20\%$ side means $+44\%$ area.
Area to side: take the square root of the factor ($1.21\to1.1$).
Money, tiles and paint scale with area, never with a side.
Map areas: square the linear scale, convert units once.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A triangle with base and height, or an equilateral triangle with its side.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Base and height given: half × base × height.
Equilateral: (√3 ÷ 4) × side × side.

example.q: Find the area of an equilateral triangle of side 12 cm.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Three sides are given but no height.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Half the sum of the sides is s.
Area = √(s × (s−a) × (s−b) × (s−c)). Check for 13, 14, 15 (area 84) first.

example.q: Find the area of a triangle with sides 13, 14 and 15 cm.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two equal sides and a base are given, but no height.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Cut it in half down the middle to get a right triangle.
Find the height, then half × base × height.

example.q: An isosceles triangle has equal sides of 17 cm and a base of 16 cm. Find its area.
example.solution:
Half base = 8, slant side = 17
Height = √(17² − 8²) = √225 = 15
Area = ½ × 16 × 15 = **120 sq cm**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Perimeter and diagonal of a rectangle are given. Area is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Half the perimeter = length + breadth.
Find two numbers that add up to it and fit the diagonal (like 5, 12, 13).

example.q: A rectangle has perimeter 34 cm and diagonal 13 cm. Find its area.
example.solution:
Length + breadth = 34 ÷ 2 = 17
5 + 12 = 17 and 5, 12, 13 fit the diagonal
Area = 5 × 12 = **60 sq cm**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Diagonals of a rhombus are given. Side or perimeter is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach:
The diagonals cut each other in half at a right angle.
Half-diagonals and the side form a right triangle.

example.q: The diagonals of a rhombus are 10 cm and 24 cm. Find its perimeter.
example.solution:
Halves are 5 and 12
Side = √(5² + 12²) = 13
Perimeter = 4 × 13 = **52 cm**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The radius, diameter, area or circumference is given. Another one is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Use 22/7 for π. Halve the diameter to get the radius.
Find the radius first, then the rest.

example.q: The circumference of a circle is 132 cm. Find its area.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A part of a circle cut by an angle at the centre. Its area or arc length is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Find the whole circle first.
Take the fraction angle ÷ 360 of it.

example.q: Find the area of a sector of angle 90° in a circle of radius 14 cm.
example.solution:
Whole circle = 22/7 × 14 × 14 = 616
90° is 90 ÷ 360 = ¼ of the circle
616 ÷ 4 = **154 sq cm**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A path around a circle, or a wheel rolling a distance.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Ring: big circle area − small circle area.
Wheel: one turn covers one circumference, so turns = distance ÷ circumference.

example.q: A wheel of diameter 70 cm rolls 231 m. How many turns does it make?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Angles, number of sides or diagonals of a regular polygon.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Outside angle = 360 ÷ number of sides.
Inside angle = 180 − outside angle.

example.q: Each inside angle of a regular polygon is 150°. How many sides does it have?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Each side is increased by 20%. How does the area change?"
pyqPatterns.approach:
Pick a simple number like 10 for the side.
Compare the old and new area.

example.q: Each side of a square is increased by 20%. By what % does the area increase?
example.solution:
Side 10 → area 100
New side 12 → area 144
Increase = 44 on 100 = **44%**

solvedExamples.q: The perimeter of a rectangle is 50 cm and its length is 5 cm more than its breadth. Find its area.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Sum 25, difference 5 → 15 and 10 directly. Area 150. Trap: 169 = $13^2$ if you misread the relation.

solvedExamples.q: Find the perimeter (in cm) of a sector of a circle of radius 7 cm with central angle $90^\circ$. [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
solvedExamples.solution:
Arc $=\frac{90}{360}\times2\times\frac{22}{7}\times7=11$ cm.

Perimeter of sector $=$ arc $+2r=11+14=25$ cm.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Quarter circle: arc 11, add two radii 14 → 25. Trap: 11 (arc only).

solvedExamples.q: A rectangular park is 60 m long and 40 m wide. A path 3 m wide is built all around it on the outside. Find the area of the path.
solvedExamples.solution:
Outer rectangle: $(60+6)\times(40+6)=66\times46=3036$ sq m.

Path area $=3036-2400=636$ sq m.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Add the width **twice** on each dimension: $66\times46-60\times40=636$. The width joins both sides of each dimension.

solvedExamples.q: If each side of an equilateral triangle is increased by 10%, then the percentage increase in its area is:
solvedExamples.solution:
Area scales as the square of the side: $1.1^2=1.21$, i.e. a 21% increase.

Equivalently, $10+10+\frac{10\times10}{100}=21\%$.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Square the factor: $(1.1)^2=1.21\Rightarrow+21\%$. Trap: 20% (ignoring the $ab/100$ term).

practice.shortcut: Sum 24, half is 12, ×8 = 96. Trap: 192 missed the half.

practice.q: The length of a rectangle increases by 20% and the breadth decreases by 10%. The percentage change in its area is:
practice.shortcut: $20-10-2=+8$. Traps: 10% (ignores the cross term), 'no change' (assumes cancellation).

practice.q: A sector of a circle has radius 14 cm and central angle $45^\circ$. Its area is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
practice.shortcut: $45^\circ=\frac18$ of a circle: $616/8=77$. Trap: 616 is the whole circle.

practice.q: The perimeter of a rhombus is 40 cm and one of its diagonals is 12 cm. The area of the rhombus is:
practice.solution:
Side $=10$ cm. Half of the given diagonal $=6$, so the other half-diagonal $=\sqrt{10^2-6^2}=8$, giving
diagonals 12 and 16. Area $=\frac12\times12\times16=96$ sq cm.
practice.shortcut: 6-8-10 triplet with the half-diagonals: other diagonal 16, area $\frac12\times12\times16=96$.

practice.q: A path 7 m wide runs around a circular park of radius 14 m. The area of the path is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
practice.solution:
Outer radius $=14+7=21$ m.

Path area $=\frac{22}{7}(21^2-14^2)=\frac{22}{7}\times245=770$ sq m.
practice.shortcut: $\frac{22}{7}\times(441-196)=770$. Trap: 616 forgets the path width.

practice.q: The diagonal of a rectangle is 25 cm and one of its sides is 15 cm. The area of the rectangle is:
practice.solution:
Other side $=\sqrt{25^2-15^2}=\sqrt{625-225}=20$ cm.

Area $=15\times20=300$ sq cm.
practice.shortcut: 15-20-25 triplet → other side 20, area 300.

practice.q: The area of the largest square that can be inscribed in a circle of radius 7 cm is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
practice.solution:
Diagonal of the square $=$ diameter $=14$ cm.

Area $=\frac{d^2}{2}=\frac{196}{2}=98$ sq cm.
practice.shortcut: $d=14$: area $=\frac{196}{2}=98$. Trap: 154 is the circle's area, 49 is $r^2$.

practice.q: A wheel of diameter 70 cm makes 300 revolutions. The distance travelled by the wheel is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
practice.shortcut: $d=0.7$ m → 2.2 m per revolution → 660 m. Trap: 6,600 m (cm-m slip).

practice.q: If the area of a square increases by 96%, then each of its sides increases by:
practice.solution: Side factor $=\sqrt{1.96}=1.4$, so the side increases by 40%.
practice.shortcut: $\sqrt{1.96}=1.4$ → 40%. Trap: 48% (half of 96) has no basis.

practice.q: The area of a regular hexagon of perimeter 36 cm is:
practice.shortcut: Six equilateral triangles: $6\times\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\times36=54\sqrt3$. Trap: $36\sqrt3$ is the equilateral area with side 6... ×6 rule forgotten halfway.

practice.q: A wire of length 88 cm is first bent in the form of a circle and then re-bent in the form of a square. The ratio of the area of the circle to the area of the square is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
practice.solution:
Circle: $2\pi r=88\Rightarrow r=14$, area $=\frac{22}{7}\times196=616$ sq cm.

Square: side $=22$, area $=484$ sq cm.

Ratio $=616:484=14:11$.
practice.shortcut: $r=14$ (since $88=2\times\frac{22}{7}\times14$), circle area 616; square side 22, area 484; divide both by 44: 14:11.

practice.q: The base of a triangle is $15$ cm and its corresponding height is $8$ cm. Its area is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac12 \times 120 = 60$. Trap: $120$ (forgot the half).

practice.q: The area of an equilateral triangle of side $12$ cm is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac{144}{4} = 36$; keep the $\sqrt3$. Trap: $72\sqrt3$ — that is $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}a^2$.

practice.q: The area of an equilateral triangle is $25\sqrt{3}$ sq cm. Its perimeter is:
practice.shortcut: $a^2 = \frac{4K}{\sqrt3} = 100$ → $a = 10$, $P = 30$ cm. Trap: $20$ cm (side doubled, not tripled).

practice.q: The sides of a triangle are $13$ cm, $14$ cm and $15$ cm. Its area is:
practice.shortcut: (13,14,15) → 84, the standard Heron family. Trap: $70$ (wrong factor order).

practice.q: The sides of a triangle are $10$ cm, $24$ cm and $26$ cm. Its area is:
practice.solution:
$10\text{-}24\text{-}26 = 5\text{-}12\text{-}13 \times 2$: right-angled, so skip Heron.

$K = \frac12 \times 10 \times 24 = 120$ sq cm.
practice.shortcut: Triplet bypass: $\frac12 \times 240 = 120$. Trap: $130$ (used the hypotenuse as a leg).

practice.q: An isosceles triangle has equal sides $17$ cm each and base $16$ cm. Its area is:
practice.shortcut: Half-base 8 → 8-15-17 → $K = 120$. Trap: $136$ ($\frac12 \times 17 \times 16$ used a leg as height).

practice.q: An isosceles triangle has equal sides of $10$ cm and base $12$ cm. Its area is:
practice.shortcut: Half-base 6, height 8 → $\frac12 \times 96 = 48$. Trap: $60$ ($\frac12 \times 10 \times 12$).

practice.q: The sides of a triangle are $13$ cm, $14$ cm and $15$ cm. Its inradius is:
practice.shortcut: $r = K/s$ with $s$ SEMI-perimeter: $84/21 = 4$. Trap: $2$ cm (divided by the full perimeter 42).

practice.q: $AD$ is a median of $\triangle ABC$ whose area is $48$ sq cm. The area of $\triangle ABD$ is:
practice.solution:
A median splits the triangle into two equal areas (equal base halves $BD = DC$, same height from $A$).

Area of $\triangle ABD = \frac{48}{2} = 24$ sq cm.
practice.shortcut: Median → exactly half: $24$. Trap: $16$/$32$ (centroid $2:1$ applies to LENGTHS, not this split).

practice.q: In a right triangle with legs $6$ cm and $8$ cm, the altitude drawn from the right angle to the hypotenuse is:
practice.shortcut: $h = \frac{ab}{c} = \frac{48}{10} = 4.8$ cm. Trap: $5$ (guessed the midpoint).

practice.q: The hypotenuse of a right triangle is $13$ cm and one leg is $5$ cm. Its area is:
practice.shortcut: Missing leg 12 → $30$ sq cm. Trap: $32.5$ ($\frac12 \times 5 \times 13$ used the hypotenuse).

practice.q: The perimeter of a rectangle is $34$ cm and the length of its diagonal is $13$ cm. The area of the rectangle is:
practice.solution:
$l + b = \frac{34}{2} = 17$; with diagonal 13, the sides are the 5-12-13 pair ($5+12 = 17$).

Area $= 5 \times 12 = 60$ sq cm.
practice.shortcut: $K = 8.5^2 - 6.5^2 = 72.25 - 42.25 = 60$. Trap: $65$ ($\frac12 \times 13 \times ...$ — diagonal is not a height).

practice.q: The area of a rectangle is $192$ sq cm and its diagonal is $20$ cm. Its perimeter is:
practice.solution:
Sides must multiply to 192 and satisfy $l^2 + b^2 = 400$: the 12-16-20 triplet works ($12 \times 16 = 192$).

$P = 2(12 + 16) = 56$ cm.
practice.shortcut: 3-4-5 ×4: sides 12, 16 → $56$ cm. Trap: testing $l=16, b=13$ etc. without the triplet check.

practice.q: One diagonal of a rhombus is $10$ cm and its side is $13$ cm. The area of the rhombus is:
practice.solution:
Half-diagonals 5 and $x$ with hypotenuse 13: $x = 12$, so the other diagonal is $24$.

$K = \frac12 \times 10 \times 24 = 120$ sq cm.
practice.shortcut: 5-12-13 halves → $d_2 = 24$ → $120$ sq cm. Trap: $130$ ($\frac12 \times 10 \times 26$).

practice.q: The diagonals of a rhombus are in the ratio $5:12$ and its area is $120$ sq cm. The perimeter of the rhombus is:
practice.solution:
$d_1 = 5k$, $d_2 = 12k$: $\frac12 \times 60k^2 = 120 \Rightarrow k^2 = 4 \Rightarrow k = 2$.

Diagonals 10 and 24 → side 13 → perimeter $52$ cm.
practice.shortcut: $30k^2 = 120$ → $k = 2$; 5-12-13 halves → $52$ cm. Trap: $48$ (side 12 from one diagonal).

practice.q: The area of a parallelogram is $120$ sq cm and its base is $15$ cm. Its height is:
practice.shortcut: $120/15 = 8$ cm. Trap: dividing the diagonal or a side instead of the base.

practice.q: Two adjacent sides of a parallelogram are $10$ cm and $8$ cm and the angle between them is $30^\circ$. Its area is:
practice.shortcut: $\sin 30^\circ = \frac12$: $40$ sq cm. Trap: $80$ (treated it as a rectangle) or $40\sqrt3$ (used $60^\circ$).

practice.q: The diagonal of a square is $10$ cm. The area of the square is:
practice.shortcut: Half of $d^2$: $50$. Trap: $100$ (side taken as the diagonal) or $50\sqrt2$ (kept an extra $\sqrt2$).

practice.q: The parallel sides of a trapezium differ by $8$ cm and the perpendicular distance between them is $6$ cm. If the area is $96$ sq cm, the longer parallel side is:
practice.solution:
Sides $a$ and $a+8$: $\frac12(a + a + 8) \times 6 = (a+4) \times 6 = 96 \Rightarrow a + 4 = 16$.

$a = 12$, longer side $= 20$ cm.
practice.shortcut: $(a+4) \times 6 = 96$ → $a = 12$ → longer $20$ cm. Trap: $12$ — that is the SHORTER side.

practice.q: The circumference of a circle of radius $7$ cm is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $2 \times 22 = 44$ cm (the 7s cancel). Trap: $154$ — that is the AREA.

practice.q: The circumference of a circle is $132$ cm. Its area is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: 132 → r 21 (the favourite triple) → area 1386. Trap: $1296$ ($36^2$ from $r=36$).

practice.q: The area of a sector of a circle of radius $14$ cm with central angle $90^\circ$ is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: Quarter of 616 = 154. Trap: $616$ (full circle) or $308$ (half).

practice.q: The length of the arc of a sector of angle $72^\circ$ in a circle of radius $35$ cm is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $\frac15$ of 220 = 44 cm. Trap: $176$ — that's the remaining major arc.

practice.q: Two concentric circles have radii $14$ cm and $7$ cm. The area of the ring between them is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $\frac{22}{7} \times 147 = 462$. Trap: $770$ ($\pi(R+r)^2$, squaring the sum).

practice.q: A wheel of diameter $70$ cm rolls a distance of $231$ m. The number of complete revolutions it makes is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $231 \div 2.2 = 105$. Trap: forgetting cm→m (getting 10500) or using $r=70$ cm.

practice.q: A circle is inscribed in a square of side $14$ cm. The area of the circle is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.solution:
Inscribed: diameter = side, so $r = 7$ cm.

$K = \frac{22}{7} \times 49 = 154$ sq cm.
practice.shortcut: $r = 7$ → 154. Trap: $308$ — that is the circumscribed circle ($r = 7\sqrt2$).

practice.q: A circle is circumscribed about a square of side $14$ cm. The area of the circle is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.solution:
Circumscribed: diameter = diagonal $= 14\sqrt2$, so $r^2 = \frac{(14\sqrt2)^2}{4} = 98$.

$K = \frac{22}{7} \times 98 = 308$ sq cm (double the inscribed case).
practice.shortcut: $K = \frac{\pi a^2}{2} = \frac{22}{7} \times 98 = 308$. Trap: $154$ (inscribed value).

practice.q: The area of a regular hexagon of side $6$ cm is:
practice.solution:
Six equilateral triangles of side 6: each has area $\frac{\sqrt3}{4} \times 36 = 9\sqrt3$.

Total $= 6 \times 9\sqrt3 = 54\sqrt3$ sq cm.
practice.shortcut: $\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}a^2 = \frac{3\sqrt3}{2} \times 36 = 54\sqrt3$. Trap: $36\sqrt3$ (four triangles, not six).

practice.q: A regular hexagon is made of six equilateral triangles. If each triangle has area $4\sqrt{3}$ sq cm, the area of the hexagon is:
practice.shortcut: Just multiply by 6: $24\sqrt3$. Trap: dividing by 6 or using 4 pieces.

practice.q: A regular polygon has perimeter $72$ cm and apothem $6$ cm. Its area is:
practice.shortcut: Half of $432$: $216$. Trap: $432$ (forgot the half).

practice.q: The perimeter of a regular hexagon is $60$ cm (side $10$ cm) and its apothem is $5\sqrt{3}$ cm. Its area is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac12 \times 60 \times 5\sqrt3 = 150\sqrt3$. Trap: $300\sqrt3$ (no halving).

practice.q: Each interior angle of a regular octagon is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac{1080}{8} = 135^\circ$ by the sum route too. Trap: $150^\circ$ (that is the dodecagon).

practice.q: The sum of the interior angles of a regular decagon is:
practice.shortcut: $8 \times 180 = 1440$. Trap: $1800^\circ$ (used $n = 12$) or per-angle value $144^\circ$.

practice.q: The number of diagonals of a regular octagon is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac{8 \times 5}{2} = 20$. Trap: $16$ (counted each diagonal once but used $n-4$).

practice.q: A polygon has $90$ diagonals. The number of sides of the polygon is:
practice.solution:
$\frac{n(n-3)}{2} = 90 \Rightarrow n(n-3) = 180$.

Factor pairs of 180 differing by 3: $15 \times 12$ → $n = 15$.
practice.shortcut: $15(15-3) = 180$ → 15 sides. Trap: $12$ (that gives 54 diagonals).

practice.q: The length of the longest diagonal of a regular hexagon of side $8$ cm is:
practice.solution: The longest diagonal passes through the centre: two radii $= 2a = 16$ cm.
practice.shortcut: $2 \times 8 = 16$ cm. Trap: $8\sqrt3$ — that is the SHORT diagonal.

practice.q: The longest diagonal of a regular hexagon is $12$ cm. The area of the hexagon is:
practice.solution:
Longest diagonal $= 2a \Rightarrow a = \frac{12}{2} = 6$ cm.

$K = \frac{3\sqrt3}{2} \times 36 = 54\sqrt3$ sq cm.
practice.shortcut: Side = half the long diagonal: $6$; area $\frac{3\sqrt3}{2} \times 36 = 54\sqrt3$. Trap: $108\sqrt3$ (took the diagonal as the side).

practice.q: The area of a square is $25$ sq cm. If each side is doubled, the new area is:
practice.solution:
Side doubles → $k = 2$ → area $\times k^2 = 4$.

New area $= 25 \times 4 = 100$ sq cm (side $10$).
practice.shortcut: $k^2 = 4$: $25 \times 4 = 100$. Trap: $50$ (doubled the area, not squared the factor).

practice.q: The perimeters of two similar triangles are in the ratio $3:5$. If the area of the larger triangle is $200$ sq cm, the area of the smaller triangle is:
practice.solution:
Area ratio $= 3^2 : 5^2 = 9 : 25$.

Smaller area $= 200 \times \frac{9}{25} = 72$ sq cm.
practice.shortcut: $\left(\frac35\right)^2 = \frac{9}{25}$: $200 \times \frac{9}{25} = 72$. Trap: $120$ (linear ratio applied to area).

practice.q: Carpeting a square room of side $5$ m costs Rs $600$. The cost of carpeting a square room of side $15$ m (same rate) is:
practice.shortcut: Area-based cost scales $k^2$: $600 \times 9 = 5400$. Trap: $1800$ (scaled by $k$, not $k^2$).

practice.q: It takes $80$ identical tiles to cover a square floor. If the side of the floor is doubled (tiles unchanged), the number of tiles needed is:
practice.solution: Side doubles → area (and tile count) $\times 4$: $80 \times 4 = 320$ tiles.
practice.shortcut: $k^2 = 4$: $320$. Trap: $160$ (doubled the count).

practice.q: If each side of a square is increased by $20\%$, the percentage increase in its area is:
If each side of a square is decreased by $10\%$, the percentage decrease in its area is:
practice.shortcut: $2(10) - \frac{10^2}{100} = 19\%$. Trap: $20\%$ (straight doubling, missing the $+x^2$ correction).

practice.q: On a map drawn to the scale $1 : 5000$, a rectangular plot measures $4$ sq cm. The actual area of the plot is:
practice.solution:
Areas scale as $n^2$: actual area $= 4 \times 5000^2 = 10^8$ sq cm.

$10^8$ sq cm $= \frac{10^8}{10^4} = 10{,}000$ sq m (= 1 hectare).
practice.shortcut: $4 \times 25{,}000{,}000$ sq cm → $10{,}000$ sq m. Trap: forgetting the unit conversion (answering $10^8$).

practice.q: A photograph is enlarged so that each dimension becomes $250\%$ of the original. If the original photo's area is $40$ sq cm, the enlarged area is:
A wire $44$ cm long is bent into a square, and an equal wire into a circle. The difference between the areas enclosed (take $\pi = 22/7$) is:
practice.solution:
Square: side $11$ → area $121$ sq cm. Circle: $r = \frac{44}{2 \times 22/7} = 7$ → area $154$ sq cm.

Difference $= 154 - 121 = 33$ sq cm.
practice.shortcut: Circle $154$ − square $121$ = $33$. Trap: $11$ (difference of sides/radii, not areas).

practice.q: Two squares have perimeters $24$ cm and $36$ cm. The difference of their areas is:
practice.solution:
Sides $6$ and $9$; areas $36$ and $81$.

Difference $= 81 - 36 = 45$ sq cm.
practice.shortcut: Sides from perimeters first: $6, 9$ → $81 - 36 = 45$. Trap: $12$ (difference of perimeters squared, $6^2$).
